title: Restorative Interior Design to Renew Attention and Reduce Stress in Small Residential Units
research_question: To identify a successful restorative environment suitable for the interior space of a small residential unit.

participants.description: University students and employed individuals (58 female, 31 male; age 18-42, mean 27) residing in urban areas of Chiang Mai, Thailand, who had experienced 7-14 days of quarantine, remote work, or online education in small living accommodations.
participants.recruitment: via social media platforms and posters

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Seven virtual models of a 20-square-meter studio-type dormitory room: one non-restorative baseline model and six restorative environments. The restorative environments were combinations of two forms (Rectilinear, Curvilinear) and three styles (Minimal, Natural, Rustic). Models were rendered in 360-degree visual view with 8k resolution quality for VR using Twinmotion software and viewed via Meta Oculus Quest 2.

measures.construct: Perceived Restorativeness (Being away, Extent, Fascination, Compatibility, Overall Perceived Restorativeness)
measures.instrument: brief Perceived Restorativeness Scale (PRS) by Felsten (2009)

findings.antecedent: Restorative interior design (Rectilinear Minimal, Curvilinear Minimal, Rectilinear Natural, Curvilinear Natural, Rectilinear Rustic, Curvilinear Rustic styles)
findings.mechanism: Restorative environments help renew attention and reduce stress.
findings.quote: each of the six restorative environment models achieved notably higher scores than the non-restorative baseline model

findings.mechanism: High coherence, consistency, and unity in design.
findings.quote: Rectilinear Minimal ... scored the highest on most components.

findings.mechanism: Harmonious blend of actual natural elements with curvilinear lines, resulting in a cohesive overall design.
findings.quote: Curvilinear Natural ... scored the highest on most components.

findings.mechanism: Lack of coherence, aesthetic complementarity, evoking feelings of being 'out of place' and unfamiliar; perceived as dark, old, or dirty.
findings.source: Table 2, Table 3, p. 12, p. 13, p. 14, p. 15
findings.quote: Rustic style models consistently scored the lowest on most components

findings.mechanism: Simple forms mimicking nature were not distinctly noticeable enough to effectively convey restorative attributes; participants did not perceive noticeable distinctions.
findings.quote: the comprehensive score for form (Rectilinear versus Curvilinear) did not reveal any significant difference (p > 0.05).

findings.mechanism: The effect of personal preference is as high as the effect of direct nature in compact settings.
findings.quote: The overall score for style (Minimal versus Natural) exhibited no substantial difference (p > 0.05).
Restorative ... demonstrated high correlations with compatibility at 0.841
Restorative ... demonstrated high correlations with ... fascination at 0.837
Restorative ... demonstrated high correlations with ... being away at 0.819
Restorative ... demonstrated high correlations with ... extent at 0.816
the overall perceived restorativeness demonstrated a strong correlation with preference at 0.890.

findings.mechanism: Preference and compatibility are primary components linked to restorative impact in small residential units.
findings.quote: the highest correlation was found between preference and compatibility at 0.912.

mechanisms: Restorative environments help renew attention and reduce stress (Attention Restoration Theory, Stress Recovery Theory).
Coherence (consistency and harmony of elements) in design enhances restorative effects, particularly for 'extent' and 'preference' components of ART.
Lack of coherence or aesthetic complementarity can evoke feelings of being 'out of place' and unfamiliar, reducing restorativeness.
Personal preference is as important as direct nature in influencing restorative outcomes in compact settings.
Simple forms mimicking nature may not be distinctly noticeable enough to convey restorative attributes.
Excessive use of plants can evoke negative feelings (messiness, dirtiness, scaring), reducing restorativeness.
Rustic style is perceived as dark, old, or dirty, reducing restorativeness.
implementation_implications: Design restorative environments for small residential units by considering individual preferences and compatibility, coherence of elements, and overall aesthetics.
Integrate direct natural elements (e.g., plants) in moderation and with attention to aesthetics to prevent negative emotions.
Crafting improved restorative environments requires more than just integrating natural elements; focus on holistic design.

limitations: Experimental environments were virtual, not physical, and graphics may have appeared artificial.
Fixed view location restricted participants' exploration and perception of distinct forms.
Participants did not experience prolonged periods of living/lockdown during the study, potentially limiting mental fatigue/stress levels.
Brief exposure to environments might not have been sufficient for long-term restoration effects.
Study examined only a specific combination of two forms and three styles, excluding other architectural forms and styles.
Study did not determine the extent to which preferences and coherence influenced restoration, nor which factors had the most significant impact.
Measurements relied solely on the Perceived Restorativeness Scale (PRS), susceptible to individual biases/preferences.
Despite color control, each model had different color schemes due to material colors (green for Natural, dark brown for Rustic, pastel for Minimal), leaving the effect of color uncertain.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The shift in lifestyle due to urbanization and the recent pandemic has increased demand for small residential units suitable for remote work and longer stays. Restorative environments have gained importance within these spaces as they impact productivity, reduce fatigue, and alleviate stress. This study aims to identify effective restorative environments for small residential units, deepening our current understanding about contributions of interior design to personal well-being. Six virtual models combining Rectilinear and Curvilinear forms with Minimal, Natural, and Rustic styles were created. A total of 89 participants with lockdown or remote work experience evaluated these environments using VR devices and a PRS questionnaire. Results showed higher ratings for all virtual restorative environments compared to the non-restorative control design. The Rectilinear form with Minimal style and Curvilinear form with Natural style received the highest ratings. Surprisingly, nature analogues using curves and natural materials did not produce expected outcomes, highlighting the importance of integrating natural elements, considering individual preferences, and ensuring environmental coherence for enhanced restorative attributes. Creating an effective restorative environment extends beyond incorporating nature-based elements. These findings offer insights for designing residential spaces that boost well-being and productivity, especially in the context of remote work and extended stays in compact residential units.
